## Method

### Study design and participants

The trial was conducted online in Germany and follows a concealed, prospective, parallel group, placebo-control trial with 1:1 randomization. The study design has been prospectively published. [@frombergerMyTabuAPlaceboControlled2021] Data on re-offenses based on criminal records will be assessed in a five-year follow up. The trial was prospectively registered on April 24, 2020 in the [German Clinical Trial Register (DRKS00021256)](https://drks.de/search/en/trial/DRKS00021256). The research project was advised by a multidisciplinary team including a representative of participants. All sexual offenders under community supervision (§§56, 57, 68 StGB) from all German federal states (except Hamburg, Bremen, and Saarland), which are sentenced for at least one case of CSA (§§176ff StGB) or CSEM (§184b StGB), were eligible. There exist no exclusion criteria regarding gender. Only persons who are older than 18 years were included. Exclusion criteria were a probation period shorter than six months at enrollment; no access to online intervention, a severe acute psychiatric or cerebro-organic disorder, or a severe cognitive impairment. All participants gave written informed consent. The participants were credited with monetary compensation (€120 when all sessions were completed). However, the participants did not receive any confirmation of having met the treatment requirements set by court . Ethics approval was granted by the medical ethical board of the University Medical Center Göttingen, Göttingen, Germany, on February 21, 2020 (reference number 16/2/20).

### Randomisation and masking

The trial comprises two parallel arms (intervention arm and placebo arm). Subjects are randomly allocated to treatment using an allocation ratio of 1:1. The randomization lists are centrally generated using a computerized system (secuTrial®, interActive Systems GmbH, Germany), stratified by the offense type (§176ff StGB vs. §184b StGB), type of community supervision (CS), external treatment in addition to community supervision as ordered by court, and static risk to re-offend at baseline (assessed with the modified Static-99 [@setoOnlineSolicitationOffenders2012]). At screening, each subject receives the next consecutive screening number. At randomization, each subject eligible for study participation receives the next consecutive randomization number according to his stratum from a block of randomization numbers (block size: 4). Due to security reasons, blinding of Supervison Officers (SOs) and Study Therapists (STs) was not possible. Nevertheless, participants, outcome adjudicators, and data analysts have been blinded until the end of the data analysis.

### Procedures

The concept of the WBI framework, theoretical foundation, and content of the WBI are published online [@frombergerMyTabuAPlaceboControlled2021] (see appendix Section 2 and Figure 1 for a detailed description). The content of the intervention and placebo arm are summarized in @tbl-module-content. The WBI builds on already established in-face community-based treatment programs following a cognitive-behavioral approach. Both treatment programs are designed for CSA as well as CSEM offenders. [@brikenPraeventionSexuellenKindesmissbrauchs2017; @wildPreventionSexualChild2020] The intervention arm focus solely on psychological meaningful risk factors. [@setoEmpiricallybasedDynamicRisk2023]

{{< pagebreak >}}

For the recruitment of participants, scientific staff informed SOs about the clinical trial and asked them to inform individuals under their supervision. If interested, a meeting with an research assistant took place at the supervision office. During this meeting, the research assistant provided detailed information about the goals and procedure of the trial, data security and advantages or disadvantages of taking part in the trial and that he had to sign an intervention agreement. In the intervention agreement, the participant agreed not to commit offenses during the participation and is informed that any violation could lead to exclusion. After obtaining the written informed consent, the research assistant extracted data for randomization and baseline characteristics from official records on site. After allocation, the username as well as the initial password necessary to log in was delivered by post to the SO, who gave it to the participant at their next meeting. After the first log-in, the participant had to go through an introduction section, before he was able to start the WBI. The WBI was divided into six modules, each module was further divided into four sessions. Participants were advised to walk through one session per week and finish one module in one month. The next session becomes unlocked, when one week has past and all guided exercises have been successfully completed. User tests before running the trial took approximately 60 minutes to complete the content of one session. Questionnaires were provided automatically at the pre-defined timepoint within the WBI online (see appendix Table 1). Due to ethical reasons, before presenting the questionnaire forms for the primary outcome and the Mood and Risk Questionnaire (MRQ), participants were informed that these answers will be viewable by their SO. Only SOs had access to this data during the trial. To prematurely exclude a participant from the clinical trial, the SO had to fill in a questionnaire on exclusion reasons. There was no time constraint defined at which a participant was excluded (e.g. if the participants needs more time than advised). Due to data security aspects, the trial staff had no possibility to contact a participant during the clinical trial directly. All communication with participants took place online within the secured in-app messenger of the WBI; communication between trial staff and SOs per Email, telephone or in presence. SOs received remember Emails, if the participant has not logged in in the past month. Additionally, SOs not logged in within one month have been automatically reminded by Email. STs (one male psychotherapist, four female psychologists) were intensively trained by completing a practice online treatment of at least one simulated participant. Regular monthly group supervisions ensured treatment consistency; the answers of STs on guided exercises were manualized (by predefined templates, see appendix Figure 2). To minimize therapist-related effects, the same therapists provided both trial arms.

### Outcomes

References, psychometric criteria and descriptions for all outcomes are provided in the appendix Section 3. Primary outcomes, as defined in the Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP), were officially recorded re-offenses five years after last-patient-out (at September 2030) and the Index of Desistance (IoD), a self-report scale. [@frombergerMyTabuAPlaceboControlled2021] However, recently, the items of the scales underlying the IoD have been reduced in order to enhance their psychometric quality; one scale (CMC) was removed due to low internal consistency and the IoD was renamed (Child Sexual Abuse Risk Evaluation Self-Report, CARES). The CARES total score is a composite measure with higher scores indicating greater severity of both acute and stable dynamic risk factors. [@sonjaetzlerDevelopmentInitialValidationsubmitted] We report the validated CARES scale instead of the pre-specified IoD due to its higher psychometric quality.

Secondary endpoints include specific questionnaires operationalizing the risk factors that are thematically addressed in the individual modules (see table X).

Frequencies of re-offenses as reported by the SOs was assessed in a structured manner (Exclusion Questionnaire (EQ)). Frequencies of recidivism or concrete preparations for recidivism as reported in in-app messages or during working on guided exercises have been assessed continuously (see appendix Figure 4). Adverse events were assessed systematically with the Mood and Risk Questionnaire (MRQ). An adverse event was post-hoc defined as the occurrence of at least one report of the highest possible score during working on the WBI. Only post measures of the MRQ were considered to assess adverse events.

Without predefined hypotheses, the Working Alliance Inventory-Short Revised (WAI-SR) was used to assess therapeutic alliance with STs and SOs on six timepoints. Changes in psychological well-being have been assessed with the WHO-5 Well-Being Index (WHO-5). To assess a possible volunteer-effect, the Questionnaire of Non-Participation (QNP) was developed to assess possible reasons for not taking part. The Questionnaire for Acceptance of Technology (ATQ) and the Questionnaire of Subjective Therapy Preconditions (SBV-R) were administered. Results of these questionnaires are not related to the hypotheses and not reported here. Preliminary data from the intermediate analysis are published with regard to the ATQ. [@schroderAcceptanceWebBasedIntervention2024; @schroderEngagementWebbasedIntervention2025]

### Statistical analysis

The statistical analysis plan (SAP) was signed off before final database lock and unmasking. Data analysis was performed using the software R [@rcoreteamLanguageEnvironmentStatistical2025] . Interim analysis was done by a independent data safety monitoring board (DSMB) on April 20, 2022. Stopping guidelines have been prospectively defined (see appendix Section 1).

A priori, a rate of 50% of screened participants taking voluntarily part in the clinical trial was assumed. Based on the estimation of responsible ministries, it was expected to see 1165 eligible participants during the recruitment period, of which 50% (582) were expected to participate in the study. Taking a dropout of 26·4% into account, it was expected to see 428 participants completing the WBI. We found no published WBI for ICCO to guide power calculation, thus sample size was calculated in order to be able to detect to small effects (d = 0·27). Power analysis revealed a minimum of 214 participants in each arm to be able to detect small effects.

To analyze the time participants needed to finish the WBI, the time span from beginning of the first module to the time finishing the consecutive modules, was analyzed by means of Gaussian linear model for repeated measures (MMRM) with treatment group, time (six time-points), and treatment-by-time interaction. Least squares mean changes from baseline are reported for the treatment groups with 95% confidence interval (CI) as well as the difference between the least squares treatment group means with 95% CI and p-value testing the null hypothesis of no treatment effect. The same analysis rationale was applied for the time, a participant was working on the content of a module.

Statistical analysis for the primary outcome was performed according to the intention-to-treat principle. (ITT). The ITT population was defined as all participants who have completed at least one module. The CARES was analyzed by MMRM with treatment group, time (six time-points), treatment-by-time interaction, and the randomization strata as factors, baseline measurements of the outcome, and the CARES as dependent variable. In an additional MMRM, time span from baseline was additionally modeled as factor. Least squares mean changes from baseline are reported for the treatment groups with 95% CI as well as the difference between the least squares treatment group means with 95% CI and p-value testing the null hypothesis of no treatment effect. A sensitivity analysis on imputed values complemented the analysis. Imputation has been done using multiple reference based imputation followed by ANCOVA models [@wolbersStandardReferencebasedConditional2022]. Exploratory, non-parametric Brunner-Munzel test a[@brunnerNonparametricBehrensFisherProblem2000] for paired data were used to compare the pre- and post-module scores within each trial arm. Additionally, differences from baseline have been compared exploratively between the treatment groups using the Brunner-Munzel test for unpaired data. [@brunnerNonparametricBehrensFisherProblem2000] If discontinuation from study was due to clear evidence for recidivism, the subject receives the maximal value for the remaining measurements.

To analyze the treatment effects of each individual module, secondary endpoints have been analyzed using the non-parametric Brunner-Munzel test for paired data [@brunnerNonparametricBehrensFisherProblem2000] comparing the pre- and post-module scores within each trial arm. Additionally, differences from baseline have been compared exploratively between the treatment groups using the Brunner-Munzel test for unpaired data. [@brunnerNonparametricBehrensFisherProblem2000] The effect of each module on the secondary endpoints was further exploratory analyzed by fitting linear models with treatment group and the randomization strata as factors, pre module scores as covariate and post module scores as dependent variable if appropriate. If necessary, the scores have been transformed before the analysis. If the assumptions of a linear model were not fulfilled either an ordinal regression model was fitted analogously instead or the score was dichotomized in order to fit a logistic regression model analogously. Analyses on the secondary endpoints were carried out on all participants who provided pre- and post data for the respective module.

Frequencies and percentages of occurrences of re-offenses as reported by the SOs and differences between arms were compared using Fisher’s exact tests. Frequencies and percentages of participants reporting at least one adverse event during working on the WBI are provided for each sub-scale of the MRQ and differences between arms were compared using Fisher’s exact tests.

Ancilliary outcomes have not been pre-sepecified. The WHO-5 was analyzed by MMRM with treatment group, time (six time-points), treatment-by-time interaction, and the randomization strata as factors, baseline measurements of the outcome and the WHO-5 total score as dependent variable. Least squares mean changes from baseline are reported for the treatment groups with 95% CI as well as the difference between the least squares group means with 95% CI and p-value testing the null hypothesis of no treatment effect. The same analysis rationale was applied for the WAI-SR COACH and WAI-SR SUPERVISOR except that time with five time-points was fitted.

For all MMRMs, The error terms were assumed to follow a multivariate normal distribution with unstructured covariance. For all multiple comparisons, p-values were adjusted using the Bonferroni-Holm’s method to control the family-wise error rate.
